div.head: ACT I
div.stage: Summer afternoon in a cottage garden on the eastern slope of a hill a little south of Haslemere in Surrey. Looking up the hill, the cottage is seen in the left hand corner of the garden, with its thatched roof and porch, and a large latticed window to the left of the porch. A paling completely shuts in the garden, except for a gate on the right. The common rises uphill beyond the paling to the sky line. Some folded canvas garden chairs are leaning against the side bench in the porch. A lady's bicycle is propped against the wall, under the window. A little to the right of the porch a hammock is slung from two posts. A big canvas umbrella, stuck in the ground, keeps the sun off the hammock, in which a young lady lies reading and making notes, her head towards the cottage and her feet towards the gate. In front of the hammock, and within reach of her hand, is a common kitchen chair, with a pile of serious-looking books and a supply of writing paper on it. A gentleman walking on the common comes into sight from behind the cottage. He is hardly past middle age, with something of the artist about him, unconventionally but carefully dressed, and clean-shaven except for a moustache, with an eager susceptible face and very amiable and considerate manners. He has silky black hair, with waves of grey and white in it. His eyebrows are white, his moustache black. He seems not certain of his way. He looks over the paling; takes stock of the place; and sees the young lady.

sp.speaker: THE GENTLEMAN
sp.p: I beg your pardon. Can you direct me to Hindhead View—Mrs Alison's?

sp.speaker: THE YOUNG LADY
sp.p: This is Mrs Alison's.

sp.speaker: THE GENTLEMAN.
sp.p: Indeed! Perhaps—may I ask are you Miss Vivie Warren?

sp.speaker: THE YOUNG LADY
sp.stage: [sharply, as she turns on her elbow to get a good look at him]
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: THE GENTLEMAN
sp.p: I'm afraid I appear intrusive. My name is Praed.
sp.stage: [Vivie at once throws her books upon the chair, and gets out of the hammock].
sp.p: Oh, pray dont let me disturb you.

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.stage: [striding to the gate and opening it for him]
sp.p: Come in, Mr Praed.
Glad to see you.
sp.stage: [She proffers her hand and takes his with a resolute and hearty grip. She is an attractive specimen of the sensible, able, highly-educated young middle-class Englishwoman. Age 22. Prompt, strong, confident, self-possessed. Plain business-like dress, but not dowdy. She wears a chatelaine at her belt, with a fountain pen and a paper knife among its pendants].

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Very kind of you indeed, Miss Warren.
sp.stage: [She shuts the gate with a vigorous slam. He passes in to the middle of the garden, exercising his fingers, which are slightly numbed by her greeting].
sp.p: Has your mother arrived?

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: Is she coming?

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: Didnt you expect us?

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Now, goodness me, I hope Ive not mistaken the day. That would be just like me, you know. Your mother arranged that she was to come down from London and that I was to come over from Horsham to be introduced to you.

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: Did she? Hm! My mother has rather a trick of taking me by surprise—to see how I behave myself when she's away, I suppose. I fancy I shall take my mother very much by surprise one of these days, if she makes arrangements that concern me without consulting me beforehand. She hasnt come.

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: I'm really very sorry.

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: It's not your fault, Mr Praed, is it? And I'm very glad youve come. You are the only one of my mother's friends I have ever asked her to bring to see me.

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: Oh, now this is really very good of you, Miss Warren!

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Will you come indoors; or would you rather sit out here and talk?

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: It will be nicer out here, dont you think?

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Then I'll go and get you a chair.
sp.stage: [She goes to the porch for a garden chair].

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: Oh, pray, pray! Allow me.

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: Take care of your fingers: theyre rather dodgy things, those chairs.
sp.stage: [She goes across to the chair with the books on it; pitches them into the hammock; and brings the chair forward with one swing].

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: Oh, now do let me take that hard chair. I like hard chairs.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: So do I. Sit down, Mr Praed.
sp.stage: [This invitation she gives with genial peremptoriness, his anxiety to please her clearly striking her as a sign of weakness of character on his part. But he does not immediately obey].

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: By the way, though, hadnt we better go to the station to meet your mother?

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: Why? She knows the way.

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: Er—I suppose she does

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Do you know, you are just like what I expected. I hope you are disposed to be friends with me.

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: Thank you, my dear Miss Warren: thank you. Dear me! I'm so glad your mother hasnt spoilt you!

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Well, in making you too conventional. You know, my dear Miss Warren, I am a born anarchist. I hate authority. It spoils the relations between parent and child: even between mother and daughter. Now I was always afraid that your mother would strain her authority to make you very conventional. It's such a relief to find that she hasnt.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Oh! have I been behaving unconventionally?

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Oh no: oh dear no. At least not conventionally unconventionally, you understand.
sp.stage: [She nods and sits down. He goes on, with a cordial outburst]
sp.p: But it was so charming of you to say that you were disposed to be friends with me! You modern young ladies are splendid: perfectly splendid!

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: Eh?
sp.stage: [watching him with dawning disappointment as to the quality of his brains and character].

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: When I was your age, young men and women were afraid of each other: there was no good fellowship. Nothing real. Only gallantry copied out of novels, and as vulgar and affected as it could be. Maidenly reserve! gentlemanly chivalry! always saying no when you meant yes! simple purgatory for shy and sincere souls.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Yes, I imagine there must have been a frightful waste of time. Especially women's time.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Oh, waste of life, waste of everything. But things are improving. Do you know, I have been in a positive state of excitement about meeting you ever since your magnificent achievements at Cambridge: a thing unheard of in my day. It was perfectly splendid, your tieing with the third wrangler. Just the right place, you know. The first wrangler is always a dreamy, morbid fellow, in whom the thing is pushed to the length of a disease.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: It doesnt pay. I wouldnt do it again for the same money!

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: The same money!

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: I did it for £50.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Fifty pounds!

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Yes. Fifty pounds. Perhaps you dont know how it was. Mrs Latham, my tutor at Newnham, told my mother that I could distinguish myself in the mathematical tripos if I went in for it in earnest. The papers were full just then of Phillipa Summers beating the senior wrangler. You remember about it, of course.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Well anyhow she did: and nothing would please my mother but that I should do the same thing. I said flatly it was not worth my while to face the grind since I was not going in for teaching; but I offered to try for fourth wrangler or thereabouts for £50. She closed with me at that, after a little grumbling; and I was better than my bargain. But I wouldnt do it again for that. £200 would have been nearer the mark.

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: Lord bless me! Thats a very practical way of looking at it.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Did you expect to find me an unpractical person?

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: But surely it's practical to consider not only the work these honors cost, but also the culture they bring.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Culture! My dear Mr Praed: do you know what the mathematical tripos means? It means grind, grind, grind for six to eight hours a day at mathematics, and nothing but mathematics. I'm supposed to know something about science; but I know nothing except the mathematics it involves. I can make calculations for engineers, electricians, insurance companies, and so on; but I know next to nothing about engineering or electricity or insurance. I dont even know arithmetic well. Outside mathematics, lawn-tennis, eating, sleeping, cycling, and walking, I'm a more ignorant barbarian than any woman could possibly be who hadnt gone in for the tripos.

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: What a monstrous, wicked, rascally system! I knew it! I felt at once that it meant destroying all that makes womanhood beautiful.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: I dont object to it on that score in the least. I shall turn it to very good account, I assure you.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Pooh! in what way?

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: I shall set up chambers in the City, and work at actuarial calculations and conveyancing. Under cover of that I shall do some law, with one eye on the Stock Exchange all the time. Ive come down here by myself to read law: not for a holiday, as my mother imagines. I hate holidays.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: You make my blood run cold. Are you to have no romance, no beauty in your life?

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: I dont care for either, I assure you.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: You cant mean that.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Oh yes I do. I like working and getting paid for it. When I'm tired of working, I like a comfortable chair, a cigar, a little whisky, and a novel with a good detective story in it.

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: I dont believe it. I am an artist; and I cant believe it: I refuse to believe it. It's only that you havnt discovered yet what a wonderful world art can open up to you.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Yes I have. Last May I spent six weeks in London with Honoria Fraser. Mamma thought we were doing a round of sightseeing together; but I was really at Honoria's chambers in Chancery Lane every day, working away at actuarial calculations for her, and helping her as well as a greenhorn could. In the evenings we smoked and talked, and never dreamt of going out except for exercise. And I never enjoyed myself more in my life. I cleared all my expenses, and got initiated into the business without a fee into the bargain.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: But bless my heart and soul, Miss Warren, do you call that discovering art?

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Wait a bit. That wasnt the beginning. I went up to town on an invitation from some artistic people in Fitzjohn's Avenue: one of the girls was a Newnham chum. They took me to the National Gallery—

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: Ah!!

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: —to the Opera—

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: Good!

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: —and to a concert where the band played all the evening: Beethoven and Wagner and so on. I wouldnt go through that experience again for anything you could offer me. I held out for civility's sake until the third day; and then I said, plump out, that I couldnt stand any more of it, and went off to Chancery Lane. Now you know the sort of perfectly splendid modern young lady I am. How do you think I shall get on with my mother?

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: Well, I hope—er—

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: It's not so much what you hope as what you believe, that I want to know.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Well, frankly, I am afraid your mother will be a little disappointed. Not from any shortcoming on your part, you know: I dont mean that. But you are so different from her ideal.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Her what?!

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Her ideal.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Do you mean her ideal of ME?

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: What on earth is it like?

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Well, you must have observed, Miss Warren, that people who are dissatisfied with their own bringing-up generally think that the world would be all right if everybody were to be brought up quite differently. Now your mother's life has been—er—I suppose you know—

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Dont suppose anything, Mr Praed. I hardly know my mother. Since I was a child I have lived in England, at school or college, or with people paid to take charge of me. I have been boarded out all my life. My mother has lived in Brussels or Vienna and never let me go to her. I only see her when she visits England for a few days. I dont complain: it's been very pleasant; for people have been very good to me; and there has always been plenty of money to make things smooth. But dont imagine I know anything about my mother. I know far less than you do.

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: In that case—
sp.stage: [He stops, quite at a loss. Then, with a forced attempt at gaiety]
sp.p: But what nonsense we are talking! Of course you and your mother will get on capitally.
sp.stage: [He rises, and looks abroad at the view].
sp.p: What a charming little place you have here!

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: Rather a violent change of subject, Mr Praed. Why wont my mother's life bear being talked about?

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Oh, you really mustnt say that. Isnt it natural that I should have a certain delicacy in talking to my old friend's daughter about her behind her back? You and she will have plenty of opportunity of talking about it when she comes.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: No: she wont talk about it either.
However, I daresay you have good reasons for telling me nothing. Only, mind this, Mr Praed. I expect there will be a battle royal when my mother hears of my Chancery Lane project.

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: I'm afraid there will.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Well, I shall win, because I want nothing but my fare to London to start there to-morrow earning my own living by devilling for Honoria. Besides, I have no mysteries to keep up; and it seems she has. I shall use that advantage over her if necessary.

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: Oh no! No, pray. Youd not do such a thing.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Then tell me why not.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: I really cannot. I appeal to your good feeling.
Besides, you may be too bold. Your mother is not to be trifled with when she's angry.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: You cant frighten me, Mr Praed. In that month at Chancery Lane I had opportunities of taking the measure of one or two women very like my mother. You may back me to win. But if I hit harder in my ignorance than I need, remember that it is you who refuse to enlighten me. Now, let us drop the subject.
sp.stage: [She takes her chair and replaces it near the hammock with the same vigorous swing as before].

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: One word, Miss Warren. I had better tell you. It's very difficult; but—

div.stage: Mrs Warren and Sir George Crofts arrive at the gate. Mrs Warren is between 40 and 50, formerly pretty, showily dressed in a brilliant hat and a gay blouse fitting tightly over her bust and flanked by fashionable sleeves. Rather spoilt and domineering, and decidedly vulgar, but, on the whole, a genial and fairly presentable old blackguard of a woman. Crofts is a tall powerfully-built man of about 50, fashionably dressed in the style of a young man. Nasal voice, reedier than might be expected from his strong frame. Clean-shaven bulldog jaws, large flat ears, and thick neck: gentlemanly combination of the most brutal types of city man, sporting man, and man about town.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Here they are.
sp.stage: [Coming to them as they enter the garden]
sp.p: How do, mater? Mr Praed's been here this half hour waiting for you.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Well, if youve been waiting, Praddy, it's your own fault: I thought youd have had the gumption to know I was coming by the 3.10 train. Vivie: put your hat on, dear: youll get sunburnt. Oh, I forgot to introduce you. Sir George Crofts: my little Vivie.

div.stage: Crofts advances to Vivie with his most courtly manner. She nods, but makes no motion to shake hands.

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: May I shake hands with a young lady whom I have known by reputation very long as the daughter of one of my oldest friends?

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.stage: [who has been looking him up and down sharply]
sp.p: If you like.
sp.stage: [She takes his tenderly proffered hand and gives it a squeeze that makes him open his eyes; then turns away and says to her mother]
sp.p: Will you come in, or shall I get a couple more chairs?
sp.stage: [She goes into the porch for the chairs].

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Well, George, what do you think of her?

sp.speaker: CROFTS
sp.p: She has a powerful fist. Did you shake hands with her, Praed?

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Yes: it will pass off presently.

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: I hope so.
sp.stage: [Vivie reappears with two more chairs. He hurries to her assistance].
sp.p: Allow me.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Let Sir George help you with the chairs, dear.

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: Here you are.
sp.stage: [She dusts her hands and turns to Mrs Warren].
sp.p: Youd like some tea, wouldnt you?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.stage: [sitting in Praed's chair and fanning herself]
sp.p: I'm dying for a drop to drink.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: I'll see about it.

div.stage: Sir George has by this time managed to unfold a chair and plant it beside Mrs Warren, on her left. He throws the other on the grass and sits down, looking dejected and rather foolish, with th handle of his stick in his mouth. Praed, still very uneasy, fidgets about the garden on their right.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Come! sit up, George; and take your stick out of your mouth.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: I think, you know—if you dont mind my saying so—that we had better get out of the habit of thinking of her as a little girl. You see she has really distinguished herself; and I'm not sure, from what I have seen of her, that she is not older than any of us.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Only listen to him, George! Older than any of us! Well, she has been stuffing you nicely with her importance.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: But young people are particularly sensitive about being treated in that way.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Yes; and young people have to get all that nonsense taken out of them, and a good deal more besides. Dont you interfere, Praddy; I know how to treat my own child as well as you do.
sp.stage: [Praed, with a grave shake of his head, walks up the garden with his hands behind his back. Mrs Warren pretends to laugh, but looks after him with perceptible concern. Then she whispers to Crofts]
sp.p: Whats the matter with him? What does he take it like that for?

sp.speaker: CROFTS
sp.p: Youre afraid of Praed.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: What! Me! Afraid of dear old Praddy! Why, a fly wouldnt be afraid of him.

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: Youre afraid of him.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: I'll trouble you to mind your own business, and not try any of your sulks on me. I'm not afraid of you, anyhow. If you cant make yourself agreeable, youd better go home.
sp.stage: [She gets up, and, turning her back on him, finds herself face to face with Praed].
sp.p: Come, Praddy, I know it was only your tender-heartedness. Youre afraid I'll bully her.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: My dear Kitty: you think I'm offended. Dont imagine that: pray dont. But you know I often notice things that escape you; and though you never take my advice, you sometimes admit afterwards that you ought to have taken it.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Well, what do you notice now?

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Only that Vivie is a grown woman. Pray, Kitty, treat her with every respect.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Respect! Treat my own daughter with respect! What next, pray!

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.stage: [appearing at the cottage door and calling to Mrs Warren]
sp.p: Mother: will you come to my room before tea?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Yes, dearie.
sp.stage: [She laughs indulgently at Praed's gravity, and pats him on the cheek as she passes him on her way to the porch].
sp.p: Dont be cross, Praddy.
sp.stage: [She follows Vivie in to the cottage].

sp.speaker: CROFTS
sp.p: I say, Praed.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: I want to ask you a rather particular question.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Certainly.
sp.stage: [He takes Mrs Warren's chair and sits close to Crofts].

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: Thats right: they might hear us from the window. Look here: did Kitty ever tell you who that girl's father is?

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Never.

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: Have you any suspicion of who it might be?

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: None.

sp.speaker: CROFTS
sp.p: I know, of course, that you perhaps might feel bound not to tell if she had said anything to you. But it's very awkward to be uncertain about it now that we shall be meeting the girl every day. We wont exactly know how we ought to feel towards her.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: What difference can that make? We take her on her own merits. What does it matter who her father was?

sp.speaker: CROFTS
sp.p: Then you know who he was?

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: I said no just now. Did you not hear me?

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: Look here, Praed. I ask you as a particular favor. If you do know
—I only say, if you know, you might at least set my mind at rest about her. The fact is, I feel attracted.

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: Oh, dont be alarmed: it's quite an innocent feeling. Thats what puzzles me about it. Why, for all I know I might be her father.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: You! Impossible!

sp.speaker: CROFTS
sp.p: You know for certain that I'm not?

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: I know nothing about it, I tell you, any more than you. But really, Crofts—oh no, it's out of the question. Theres not the least resemblance.

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: As to that, theres no resemblance between her and her mother that I can see. I suppose she's not your daughter, is she?

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: Really, Crofts—!

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: No offence, Praed. Quite allowable as between two men of the world.

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.stage: [recovering himself with an effort and speaking gently and gravely]
sp.p: Now listen to me, my dear Crofts.

I have nothing to do with that side of Mrs Warren's life, and never had. She has never spoken to me about it; and of course I have never spoken to her about it. Your delicacy will tell you that a handsome woman needs some friends who are not—well, not on that footing with her. The effect of her own beauty would become a torment to her if she could not escape from it occasionally. You are probably on much more confidential terms with Kitty than I am. Surely you can ask her the question yourself.

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: I have asked her, often enough. But she's so determined to keep the child all to herself that she would deny that it ever had a father if she could.
I'm thoroughly uncomfortable about it, Praed.

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: Well, as you are, at all events, old enough to be her father, I dont mind agreeing that we both regard Miss Vivie in a parental way, as a young girl whom we are bound to protect and help. What do you say?

sp.speaker: CROFTS
sp.p: I'm no older than you, if you come to that.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Yes you are, my dear fellow: you were born old. I was born a boy: Ive never been able to feel the assurance of a grown-up man in my life.
sp.stage: [He folds his chair and carries it to the porch].

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Prad-dee! George! Tea-ea-ea-ea!

sp.speaker: CROFTS
sp.p: She's calling us.

div.stage: Praed shakes his head bodingly, and is following Crofts when he is hailed by a young gentleman who has just appeared on the common, and is making for the gate. He is pleasant, pretty, smartly dressed, cleverly good-for-nothing, not long turned 20, with a charming voice and agreeably disrespectful manners. He carries a light sporting magazine rifle.

sp.speaker: THE YOUNG GENTLEMAN.
sp.p: Hallo! Praed!

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Why, Frank Gardner!
sp.stage: [Frank comes in and shakes hands cordially].
sp.p: What on earth are you doing here?

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Staying with my father.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: The Roman father?

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: He's rector here. I'm living with my people this autumn for the sake of economy. Things came to a crisis in July: the Roman father had to pay my debts. He's stony broke in consequence; and so am I. What are you up to in these parts? Do you know the people here?

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Yes: I'm spending the day with a Miss Warren.

sp.speaker: FRANK
sp.p: What! Do you know Vivie? Isnt she a jolly girl? I'm teaching her to shoot with this
I'm so glad she knows you: youre just the sort of fellow she ought to know.
sp.stage: [He smiles, and raises the charming voice almost to a singing tone as he exclaims]
sp.p: It's ever so jolly to find you here, Praed.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: I'm an old friend of her mother. Mrs Warren brought me over to make her daughter's acquaintance.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: The mother! Is she here?

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Yes: inside, at tea.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Prad-dee-ee-ee-eee! The tea-cake'll be cold.

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: Yes, Mrs Warren. In a moment. Ive just met a friend here.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: A what?

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: A friend.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Bring him in.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: All right.
Will you accept the invitation?

sp.speaker: FRANK
sp.p: Is that Vivie's mother?

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: By Jove! What a lark! Do you think she'll like me?

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Ive no doubt youll make yourself popular, as usual. Come in and try

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Stop a bit.
I want to take you into my confidence.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Pray dont. It's only some fresh folly, like the barmaid at Redhill.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: It's ever so much more serious than that. You say youve only just met Vivie for the first time?

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: FRANK
sp.p: Then you can have no idea what a girl she is. Such character! Such sense! And her cleverness! Oh, my eye, Praed, but I can tell you she is clever! And—need I add?—she loves me.

sp.speaker: CROFTS
sp.stage: [putting his head out of the window]
sp.p: I say, Praed: what are you about? Do come along.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Hallo! Sort of chap that would take a prize at a dog show, aint he? Who's he?

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Sir George Crofts, an old friend of Mrs Warren's. I think we had better come in.

div.stage: On their way to the porch they are interrupted by a call from the gate. Turning, they see an elderly clergyman looking over it.

sp.speaker: THE CLERGYMAN
sp.p: Frank!

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Hallo!
The Roman father.
Yes, gov'nor: all right: presently.
Look here, Praed: youd better go in to tea. I'll join you directly.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Very good.

div.stage: The clergyman remains outside the gate, with his hands on the top of it. The Rev. Samuel Gardner, a beneficed clergyman of the Established Church, is over 50. Externally he is pretentious, booming, noisy, important. Really he is that obsolescent social phenomenon the fool of the family dumped on the Church by his father the patron, clamorously asserting himself as father and clergyman without being able to command respect in either capacity.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Well, sir. Who are your friends here, if I may ask?

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Oh, it's all right, gov'nor! Come in.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: No, sir; not until I know whose garden I am entering.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: It's all right. It's Miss Warren's.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: I have not seen her at church since she came.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Of course not: she's a third wrangler. Ever so intellectual. Took a higher degree than you did; so why should she go to hear you preach?

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Dont be disrespectful, sir.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Oh, it dont matter: nobody hears us. Come in.
sp.stage: [He opens the gate, unceremoniously pulling his father with it into the garden].
sp.p: I want to introduce you to her. Do you remember the advice you gave me last July, gov'nor?

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Yes. I advised you to conquer your idleness and flippancy, and to work your way into an honorable profession and live on it and not upon me.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: No: thats what you thought of afterwards. What you actually said was that since I had neither brains nor money, I'd better turn my good looks to account by marrying somebody with both. Well, look here, Miss Warren has brains: you cant deny that.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Brains are not everything.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: No, of course not: theres the money—

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: I was not thinking of money sir. I was speaking of higher things. Social position, for instance.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: I dont care a rap about that.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: But I do, sir.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Well, nobody wants you to marry her. Anyhow she has what amounts to a high Cambridge degree; and she seems to have as much money as she wants.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.stage: [sinking into a feeble vein of humor]
sp.p: I greatly doubt whether she has as much money as you will want.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Oh, come: I havnt been so very extravagant. I live ever so quietly; I dont drink; I dont bet much; and I never go regularly on the razzle-dazzle as you did when you were my age.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Silence, sir.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Well, you told me yourself, when I was making ever such an ass of myself about the barmaid at Redhill, that you once offered a woman £50 for the letters you wrote to her when—

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Sh-sh-sh, Frank, for Heaven's sake!
sp.stage: [He looks round apprehensively. Seeing no one within earshot he plucks up courage to boom again, but more subduedly].
sp.p: You are taking an ungentlemanly advantage of what I confided to you for your own good, to save you from an error you would have repented all your life long. Take warning by your father's follies, sir; and dont make them an excuse for your own.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Did you ever hear the story of the Duke of Wellington and his letters?

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: No, sir; and I dont want to hear it.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: The old Iron Duke didnt throw away £50: not he. He just wrote: ‘Dear Jenny: publish and be damned! Yours affectionately, Wellington.’ Thats what you should have done.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Frank, my boy: when I wrote those letters I put myself into that woman's power. When I told you about them I put myself, to some extent, I am sorry to say, in your power. She refused my money with these words, which I shall never forget. ‘Knowledge is power,’ she said; ‘and I never sell power’. Thats more than twenty years ago; and she has never made use of her power or caused me a moment's uneasiness. You are behaving worse to me than she did, Frank.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Oh yes I dare say! Did you ever preach at her the way you preach at me every day?

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: I leave you, sir. You are incorrigible.

sp.speaker: FRANK
sp.p: Tell them I shant be home to tea, will you, gov'nor, like a good fellow?
sp.stage: [He moves towards the cottage door and is met by Praed and Vivie coming out].

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: Is that your father, Frank? I do so want to meet him.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Certainly.
Gov'nor. Youre wanted.
sp.stage: [The parson turns at the gate, fumbling nervously at his hat. Praed crosses the garden to the opposite side, beaming in anticipation of civilities].
sp.p: My father: Miss Warren.

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.stage: [going to the clergyman and shaking his hand]
sp.p: Very glad to see you here, Mr Gardner.
Mother: come along: youre wanted.

div.stage: Mrs Warren appears on the threshold, and is immediately transfixed recognizing the clergyman.

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: Let me introduce—

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Why, it's Sam Gardner, gone into the Church! Well, I never! Dont you know us, Sam? This is George Crofts, as large as life and twice as natural. Dont you remember me?

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: I really—er—

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Of course you do. Why, I have a whole album of your letters still: I came across them, only the other day.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Miss Vavasour, I believe.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.stage: [correcting him quickly in a loud whisper]
sp.p: Tch! Nonsense! Mrs Warren: dont you see my daughter there?

div.head: ACT II
div.stage: Inside the cottage after nightfall. Looking eastward from within instead of westward from without, the latticed window, with its curtains drawn, is now seen in the middle of the front wall of the cottage, with the porch door to the left of it. In the left-hand side wall is the door leading to the kitchen. Farther back against the same wall is a dresser with a candle and matches on it, and Frank's rifle standing beside them, with the barrel resting in the plate-rack. In the centre a table stands with a lighted lamp on it. Vivie's books and writing materials are on a table to the right of the window, against the wall. The fireplace is on the right, with a settle: there is no fire. Two of the chairs are set right and left of the table. The cottage door opens, shewing a fine starlit night without; and Mrs Warren, her shoulders wrapped in a shawl borrowed from Vivie, enters, followed by Frank, who throws his cap on the window seat. She has had enough of walking, and gives a gasp of relief as she unpins her hat; takes it off; sticks the pin through the crown; and puts it on the table.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: O Lord! I dont know which is the worst of the country, the walking or the sitting at home with nothing to do. I could do with a whisky and soda now very well, if only they had such a thing in this place.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Perhaps Vivie's got some.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Nonsense! What would a young girl like her be doing with such things! Never mind: it dont matter. I wonder how she passes her time here! I'd a good deal rather be in Vienna.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Let me take you there.
sp.stage: [He helps her to take off her shawl, gallantly giving her shoulders a very perceptible squeeze as he does so].

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Ah! would you? I'm beginning to think youre a chip of the old block.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Like the gov'nor, eh?
sp.stage: [He hangs the shawl on the nearest chair and sits down].

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Never you mind. What do you know about such things? Youre only a boy.
sp.stage: [She goes to the hearth, to be farther from temptation].

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Do come to Vienna with me? It'd be ever such larks.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: No, thank you. Vienna is no place for you—at least not until youre a little older.
sp.stage: [She nods at him to emphasize this piece of advice. He makes a mock-piteous face, belied by his laughing eyes. She looks at him; then comes back to him].
sp.p: Now, look here, little boy
sp.stage: [taking his face in her hands and turning it up to her]:
sp.p: I know you through and through by your likeness to your father, better than you know yourself. Dont you go taking any silly ideas into your head about me. Do you hear?

sp.speaker: FRANK
sp.p: Cant help it, my dear Mrs Warren: it runs in the family.

div.stage: She pretends to box his ears; then looks at the pretty laughing upturned face for a moment, tempted. At last she kisses him, and immediately turns away, out of patience with herself.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: There! I shouldnt have done that. I am wicked. Never mind, my dear: it's only a motherly kiss. Go and make love to Vivie.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: So I have.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.stage: [turning on him with a sharp note of alarm in her voice]
sp.p: What!

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Vivie and I are ever such chums.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: What do you mean? Now see here: I wont have any young scamp tampering with my little girl. Do you hear? I wont have it.

sp.speaker: FRANK
sp.p: My dear Mrs Warren: dont you be alarmed. My intentions are honorable: ever so honorable; and your little girl is jolly well able to take care of herself. She dont need looking after half so much as her mother. She aint so handsome, you know.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Well, you have got a nice healthy two inches thick of cheek all over you. I dont know where you got it. Not from your father, anyhow.

sp.speaker: CROFTS
sp.p: The gipsies, I suppose?

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: The broomsquires are far worse.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: S-sh! Remember! youve had your warning.

div.stage: Crofts and the Reverend Samuel come in from the garden, the clergyman continuing his conversation as he enters.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: The perjury at the Winchester assizes is deplorable.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Well? what became of you two? And wheres Praddy and Vivie?

sp.speaker: CROFTS
sp.stage: [putting his hat on the settle and his stick in the chimney corner]
sp.p: They went up the hill. We went to the village. I wanted a drink.
sp.stage: [He sits down on the settle, putting his legs up along the seat].

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Well, she oughtnt go off like that without telling me.
Get your father a chair, Frank: where are your manners?
sp.stage: [Frank springs up and gracefully offers his father his chair; then takes another from the wall and sits down at the table, in the middle, with his father on his right and Mrs Warren on his left].
sp.p: George: where are you going to stay tonight? You cant stay here. And whats Praddy going to do?

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: Gardner'll put me up.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Oh, no doubt youve taken care of yourself! But what about Praddy?

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: Dont know. I suppose he can sleep at the inn.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Havnt you room for him, Sam?

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Well—er—you see, as rector here, I am not free to do as I like. Er—what is Mr Praed's social position?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Oh, he's all right: he's an architect. What an old stick-in-the-mud you are, Sam!

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Yes, it's all right, gov'nor. He built that place down in Wales for the Duke. Caernarvon Castle they call it. You must have heard of it.
sp.stage: [He winks with lightning smartness at Mrs Warren, and regards his father blandly].

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Oh, in that case, of course we shall only be too happy. I suppose he knows the Duke personally.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Oh, ever so intimately! We can stick him in Georgina's old room.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Well, thats settled. Now if those two would only come in and let us have supper. Theyve no right to stay out after dark like this.

sp.speaker: CROFTS
sp.p: What harm are they doing you?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Well, harm or not, I dont like it.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Better not wait for them, Mrs Warren. Praed will stay out as long as possible. He has never known before what it is to stray over the heath on a summer night with my Vivie.

sp.speaker: CROFTS
sp.p: I say, you know! Come!

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.stage: [rising, startled out of his professional manner into real force and sincerity]
sp.p: Frank, once for all, it's out of the question. Mrs Warren will tell you that it's not to be thought of.

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: Of course not.

sp.speaker: FRANK
sp.p: Is that so, Mrs Warren?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Well, Sam, I dont know. If the girl wants to get married, no good can come of keeping her unmarried.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: But married to him!—your daughter to my son! Only think: it's impossible.

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: Of course it's impossible. Dont be a fool, Kitty.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Why not? Isnt my daughter good enough for your son?

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: But surely, my dear Mrs Warren, you know the reasons—

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: I know no reasons. If you know any, you can tell them to the lad, or to the girl, or to your congregation, if you like.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: You know very well that I couldnt tell anyone the reasons. But my boy will believe me when I tell him there are reasons.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Quite right, Dad: he will. But has your boy's conduct ever been influenced by your reasons?

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: You cant marry her; and thats all about it.
sp.stage: [He gets up and stands on the hearth, with his back to the fireplace, frowning determinedly].

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: What have you got to do with it, pray?

sp.speaker: FRANK
sp.p: Precisely what I was going to ask myself, in my own graceful fashion.

sp.speaker: CROFTS
sp.p: I suppose you dont want to marry the girl to a man younger than herself and without either a profession or twopence to keep her on. Ask Sam, if you dont believe me.
How much more money are you going to give him?

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Not another penny. He has had his patrimony and he spent the last of it in July.

sp.speaker: CROFTS
sp.p: There! I told you.
sp.stage: [He resumes his place on the settle and puts up his legs on the seat again, as if the matter were finally disposed of].

sp.speaker: FRANK
sp.p: This is ever so mercenary. Do you suppose Miss Warren's going to marry for money? If we love one another—

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Thank you. Your love's a pretty cheap commodity, my lad. If you have no means of keeping a wife, that settles it: you cant have Vivie.

sp.speaker: FRANK
sp.p: What do you say, gov'nor, eh?

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: I agree with Mrs Warren.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: And good old Crofts has already expressed his opinion.

sp.speaker: CROFTS
sp.p: Look here: I want none of your cheek.

sp.speaker: FRANK
sp.p: I'm ever so sorry to surprise you, Crofts, but you allowed yourself the liberty of speaking to me like a father a moment ago. One father is enough, thank you.

sp.speaker: CROFTS
sp.p: Yah!

sp.speaker: FRANK
sp.p: Mrs Warren: I cannot give my Vivie up, even for your sake.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Young scamp!

sp.speaker: FRANK
sp.p: And as you no doubt intend to hold out other prospects to her, I shall lose no time in placing my case before her.
sp.stage: [They stare at him, and he begins to declaim gracefully]
sp.p: He either fears his fate too much, Or his deserts are small, That dares not put it to the touch To gain or lose it all.

div.stage: The cottage door opens whilst he is reciting; and Vivie and Praed come in. He breaks off. Praed puts his hat on the dresser. There is an immediate improvement in the company's behavior. Crofts takes down his legs from the settle and pulls himself together as Praed joins him at the fireplace. Mrs Warren loses her ease of manner and takes refuge in querulousness.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Wherever have you been, Vivie?

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.stage: [taking off her hat and throwing it carelessly on the table]
sp.p: On the hill.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Well, you shouldnt go off like that without letting me know. How could I tell what had become of you? And night coming on too!

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.stage: [going to the door of the kitchen and opening it, ignoring her mother]
sp.p: Now, about supper?
We shall be rather crowded in here, I'm afraid.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Did you hear what I said, Vivie?

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: Yes, mother.
How many are we?
One, two, three, four, five, six. Well, two will have to wait until the rest are done: Mrs Alison has only plates and knives for four.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Oh, it doesnt matter about me. I—

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: You have had a long walk and are hungry, Mr Praed: you shall have your supper at once. I can wait myself. I want one person to wait with me. Frank: are you hungry?

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Not the least in the world. Completely off my peck, in fact.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Neither are you, George. You can wait.

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: Oh, hang it, Ive eaten nothing since tea-time. Cant Sam do it?

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Would you starve my poor father?

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Allow me to speak for myself, sir. I am perfectly willing to wait.

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: Theres no need. Only two are wanted.
sp.stage: [She opens the door of the kitchen].
sp.p: Will you take my mother in, Mr Gardner.
sp.stage: [The parson takes Mrs Warren; and they pass into the kitchen. Praed and Crofts follow. All except Praed dearly disapprove of the arrangement, but do not know how to resist it. Vivie stands at the door looking in at them].
sp.p: Can you squeeze past to that corner, Mr Praed: it's rather a tight fit. Take care of your coat against the white-wash: thats right. Now, are you all comfortable?

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: Quite, thank you.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Leave the door open, dearie.
sp.stage: [Vivie frowns; but Frank checks her with a gesture, and steals to the cottage door, which he softly sets wide open].
sp.p: Oh Lor, what a draught! Youd better shut it, dear.

div.stage: Vivie shuts it with a slam, and then, noting with disgust that her mother's hat and shawl are lying about, takes them tidily to the window seat, whilst Frank noiselessly shuts the cottage door.

sp.speaker: FRANK
sp.p: Aha! Got rid of em. Well, Vivvums: what do you think of my governor?

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: Ive hardly spoken to him. He doesnt strike me as being a particularly able person.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Well, you know, the old man is not altogether such a fool as he looks. You see, he was shoved into the Church rather; and in trying to live up to it he makes a much bigger ass of himself than he really is. I dont dislike him as much as you might expect. He means well. How do you think youll get on with him?

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: I dont think my future life will be much concerned with him, or with any of that old circle of my mother's, except perhaps Praed.
What do you think of my mother?

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Really and truly?

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Yes, really and truly.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Well, she's ever so jolly. But she's rather a caution, isnt she? And Crofts! oh, my eye, Crofts!

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: What a lot, Frank!

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: What a crew!

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: If I thought that I was like that—that I was going to be a waster, shifting along from one meal to another with no purpose, and no character, and no grit in me, I'd open an artery and bleed to death without one moment's hesitation.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Oh no, you wouldnt. Why should they take any grind when they can afford not to? I wish I had their luck. No: what I object to is their form. It isnt the thing: it's slovenly, ever so slovenly.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Do you think your form will be any better when youre as old as Crofts, if you dont work?

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Of course I do. Ever so much better. Vivvums mustnt lecture: her little boy's incorrigible.
sp.stage: [He attempts to take her face caressingly in his hands].

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: Off with you: Vivvums is not in a humor for petting her little boy this evening.
sp.stage: [She rises and comes forward to the other side of the room].

sp.speaker: FRANK
sp.p: How unkind!

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: Be serious. I'm serious.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Good. Let us talk learnedly. Miss Warren: do you know that all the most advanced thinkers are agreed that half the diseases of modern civilization are due to starvation of the affections in the young. Now, I—

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: You are very tiresome.
Have you room for Frank there? He's complaining of starvation.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Of course there is
sp.stage: [clatter of knives and glasses as she moves the things on the table].
sp.p: Here! theres room now beside me. Come along, Mr Frank.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Her little boy will be ever so even with his Vivvums for this.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Here, Vivie: come on you too, child. You must be famished.
sp.stage: [She enters, followed by Crofts, who holds the door open for Vivie with marked deference. She goes out without looking at him; and shuts the door after her].
sp.p: Why, George, you cant be done: youve eaten nothing. Is there anything wrong with you?

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: Oh, all I wanted was a drink.
sp.stage: [He thrusts his hands in his pockets, and begins prowling about the room, restless and sulky].

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Well, I like enough to eat. But a little of that cold beef and cheese and lettuce goes a long way.
sp.stage: [With a sigh of only half repletion she sits down lazily on the settle].

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: What do you go encouraging that young pup for?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Now see here, George: what are you up to about that girl? Ive been watching your way of looking at her. Remember: I know you and what your looks mean.

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: Theres no harm in looking at her, is there?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: I'd put you out and pack you back to London pretty soon if I saw any of your nonsense. My girl's little finger is more to me than your whole body and soul.
sp.stage: [Crofts receives this with a sneering grin. Mrs Warren, flushing a little at her failure to impose on him in the character of a theatrically devoted mother, adds in a lower key]
sp.p: Make your mind easy: the young pup has no more chance than you have.

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: Maynt a man take an interest in a girl?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Not a man like you.

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: How old is she?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Never you mind how old she is.

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: Why do you make such a secret of it?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Because I choose.

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: Well, I'm not fifty yet; and my property is as good as ever it was—

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Yes; because youre as stingy as youre vicious.

sp.speaker: CROFTS
sp.p: And a baronet isnt to be picked up every day. No other man in my position would put up with you for a mother-in-law. Why shouldnt she marry me?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: You!

sp.speaker: CROFTS.
sp.p: We three could live together quite comfortably: I'd die before her and leave her a bouncing widow with plenty of money. Why not? It's been growing in my mind all the time Ive been walking with that fool inside there.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Yes: it's the sort of thing that would grow in your mind.

div.stage: He halts in his prowling; and the two look at one another, she steadfastly, with a sort of awe behind her contemptuous disgust: he stealthily, with a carnal gleam in his eye and a loose grin.

sp.speaker: CROFTS
sp.stage: [suddenly becoming anxious and urgent as he sees no sign of sympathy in her]
sp.p: Look here, Kitty: youre a sensible woman: you neednt put on any moral airs. I'll ask no more questions; and you need answer none. I'll settle the whole property on her; and if you want a cheque for yourself on the wedding day, you can name any figure you like—in reason.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: So it's come to that with you, George, like all the other worn-out old creatures!

sp.speaker: CROFTS
sp.p: Damn you!

div.stage: Before she can retort the door of the kitchen is opened; and the voices of the others are heard returning. Crofts, unable to recover his presence of mind, hurries out of the cottage. The clergyman appears at the kitchen door.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Where is Sir George?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Gone out to have a pipe.
sp.stage: [The clergyman takes his hat from the table, and joins Mrs Warren at the fireside. Meanwhile Vivie comes in, followed by Frank, who collapses into the nearest chair with an air of extreme exhaustion. Mrs Warren looks round at Vivie and says, with her affection of maternal patronage even more forced than usual]
sp.p: Well, dearie: have you had a good supper?

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: You know what Mrs Alison's suppers are.
sp.stage: [She turns to Frank and pets him].
sp.p: Poor Frank! was all the beef gone? did it get nothing but bread and cheese and ginger beer?
sp.stage: [Seriously, as if she had done quite enough trifling for one evening]
sp.p: Her butter is really awful. I must get some down from the stores.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Do, in Heaven's name!

div.stage: Vivie goes to the writing-table and makes a memorandum to order the butter. Praed comes in from the kitchen, putting up his handkerchief, which he has been using as a napkin.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Frank, my boy: it is time for us to be thinking of home. Your mother does not know yet that we have visitors.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: I'm afraid we're giving trouble.

sp.speaker: FRANK
sp.p: Not the least in the world: my mother will be delighted to see you. She's a genuinely intellectual artistic woman; and she sees nobody here from one year's end to another except the gov'nor; so you can imagine how jolly dull it pans out for her.

Youre not intellectual or artistic: are you, pater? So take Praed home at once; and I'll stay here and entertain Mrs Warren. Youll pick up Crofts in the garden. He'll be excellent company for the bull-pup.

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.stage: [taking his hat from the dresser, and coming close to Frank]
sp.p: Come with us, Frank. Mrs Warren has not seen Miss Vivie for a long time; and we have prevented them from having a moment together yet.

sp.speaker: FRANK
sp.stage: [quite softened and looking at Praed with romantic admiration]
sp.p: Of course. I forgot. Ever so thanks for reminding me. Perfect gentleman, Praddy. Always were. My ideal through life.
sp.stage: [He rises to go, but pauses a moment between the two older men, and puts his hand on Praed's shoulder].
sp.p: Ah, if you had only been my father instead of this unworthy old man!
sp.stage: [He puts his other hand on his father's shoulder].

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Silence, sir, silence: you are profane.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: You should keep him in better order, Sam. Goodnight. Here: take George his hat and stick with my compliments.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Goodnight.
sp.stage: [They shake hands. As he passes Vivie he shakes hands with her also and bids her goodnight. Then, in booming command, to Frank]
sp.p: Come along, sir, at once.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Byebye, Praddy.

sp.speaker: PRAED.
sp.p: Byebye, Kitty.

div.stage: They shake hands affectionately and go out together, she accompanying him to the garden gate.

sp.speaker: FRANK
sp.p: Kissums?

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: No. I hate you.
sp.stage: [She takes a couple of books and some paper from the writing-table, and sits down with them at the middle table, at the end next the fireplace].

sp.speaker: FRANK
sp.p: Sorry.
sp.stage: [He goes for his cap and rifle. Mrs Warren returns. He takes her hand]
sp.p: Goodnight, dear Mrs Warren.
sp.stage: [He kisses her hand. She snatches it away, her lips tightening, and looks more than half disposed to box his ears. He laughs mischievously and runs off, clapping-to the door behind him].

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.stage: [resigning herself to an evening of boredom now that the men are gone]
sp.p: Did you ever in your life hear anyone rattle on so? Isnt he a tease?
Now that I think of it, dearie, dont you go encouraging him. I'm sure he's a regular good-for-nothing.

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: I'm afraid so. Poor Frank! I shall have to get rid of him; but I shall feel sorry for him, though he's not worth it. That man Crofts does not seem to me to be good for much either: is he?
sp.stage: [She throws the books on the table rather roughly].

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: What do you know of men, child, to talk that way about them? Youll have to make up your mind to see a good deal of Sir George Crofts, as he's a friend of mine.

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: Why?
sp.stage: [She sits down and opens a book].
sp.p: Do you expect that we shall be much together? You and I, I mean?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Of course: until youre married. Youre not going back to college again.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Do you think my way of life would suit you? I doubt it.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Your way of life! What do you mean?

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.stage: [cutting a page of her book with the paper knife on her chatelaine]
sp.p: Has it really never occurred to you, mother, that I have a way of life like other people?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: What nonsense is this youre trying to talk? Do you want to shew your independence, now that youre a great little person at school? Dont be a fool, child.

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: Thats all you have to say on the subject, is it, mother?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Dont you keep on asking me questions like that.
Hold your tongue.
sp.stage: [Vivie works on, losing no time, and saying nothing].
sp.p: You and your way of life, indeed! What next?
sp.stage: [She looks at Vivie again. No reply].
sp.p: Your way of life will be what I please, so it will.
Ive been noticing these airs in you ever since you got that tripos or whatever you call it. If you think I'm going to put up with them youre mistaken; and the sooner you find it out, the better.
All I have to say on the subject, indeed!
Do you know who youre speaking to, Miss?

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.stage: [looking across at her without raising her head from her book]
sp.p: No. Who are you? What are you?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: You young imp!

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Everybody knows my reputation, my social standing, and the profession I intend to pursue. I know nothing about you. What is that way of life which you invite me to share with you and Sir George Crofts, pray?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Take care. I shall do something I'll be sorry for after, and you too.

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.stage: [putting aside her books with cool decision]
sp.p: Well, let us drop the subject until you are better able to face it.

You want some good walks and a little lawn tennis to set you up. You are shockingly out of condition: you were not able to manage twenty yards uphill today without stopping to pant; and your wrists are mere rolls of fat. Look at mine.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.stage: [after looking at her helplessly, begins to whimper]
sp.p: Vivie—

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: Now pray dont begin to cry. Anything but that. I really cannot stand whimpering. I will go out of the room if you do.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Oh, my darling, how can you be so hard on me? Have I no rights over you as your mother?

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Are you my mother?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Am I your mother! Oh, Vivie!

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Then where are our relatives? my father? our family friends? You claim the rights of a mother: the right to call me fool and child; to speak to me as no woman in authority over me at college dare speak to me; to dictate my way of life; and to force on me the acquaintance of a brute whom any one can see to be the most vicious sort of London man about town. Before I give myself the trouble to resist such claims, I may as well find out whether they have any real existence.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Oh no, no. Stop, stop. I am your mother: I swear it. Oh, you cant mean to turn on me—my own child! it's not natural. You believe me, dont you? Say you believe me.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Who was my father?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: You dont know what youre asking. I cant tell you.

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: Oh yes you can, if you like. I have a right to know; and you know very well that I have that right. You can refuse to tell me, if you please; but if you do, you will see the last of me tomorrow morning.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Oh, it's too horrible to hear you talk like that. You wouldnt—you couldnt leave me.

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: Yes, without a moment's hesitation, if you trifle with me about this.
How can I feel sure that I may not have the contaminated blood of that brutal waster in my veins?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: No, no. On my oath it's not he, nor any of the rest that you have ever met. I'm certain of that, at least.

div.stage: Vivie's eyes fasten sternly on her mother as the significance of this flashes on her.

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: You are certain of that, at least. Ah! You mean that that is all you are certain of.
I see.
sp.stage: [Mrs Warren buries her face in her hands].
sp.p: Dont do that, mother: you know you dont feel it a bit.
sp.stage: [Mrs Warren takes down her hands and looks up deplorably at Vivie, who takes out her watch and says]
sp.p: Well, that is enough for tonight. At what hour would you like breakfast? Is half-past eight too early for you?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: My God, what sort of woman are you?

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: The sort the world is mostly made of, I should hope. Otherwise I dont understand how it gets its business done. Come
sp.stage: [taking her mother by the wrist, and pulling her up pretty resolutely]:
sp.p: pull yourself together. Thats right.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Youre very rough with me, Vivie.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Nonsense. What about bed? It's past ten.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Whats the use of my going to bed? Do you think I could sleep?

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Why not? I shall.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: You! youve no heart.
sp.stage: [She suddenly breaks out vehemently in her natural tongue—the dialect of a woman of the people—with all her affectations of maternal authority and conventional manners gone, and an overwhelming inspiration of true conviction and scorn in her]
sp.p: Oh, I wont bear it: I wont put up with the injustice of it. What right have you to set yourself up above me like this? You boast of what you are to me—to me, who gave you the chance of being what you are. What chance had I? Shame on you for a bad daughter and a stuck-up prude!

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.stage: [sitting down with a shrug, no longer confident; for her replies, which have sounded sensible and strong to her so far, now begin to ring rather woodenly and even priggishly against the new tone of her mother]
sp.p: Dont think for a moment I set myself above you in any way. You attacked me with the conventional authority of a mother: I defended myself with the conventional superiority of a respectable woman. Frankly, I am not going to stand any of your nonsense; and when you drop it I shall not expect you to stand any of mine. I shall always respect your right to your own opinions and your own way of life.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: My own opinions and my own way of life! Listen to her talking! Do you think I was brought up like you? able to pick and choose my own way of life? Do you think I did what I did because I liked it, or thought it right, or wouldnt rather have gone to college and been a lady if I'd had the chance?

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Everybody has some choice, mother. The poorest girl alive may not be able to choose between being Queen of England or Principal of Newnham; but she can choose between ragpicking and flowerselling, according to her taste. People are always blaming their circumstances for what they are. I dont believe in circumstances. The people who get on in this world are the people who get up and look for the circumstances they want, and, if they cant find them, make them.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Oh, it's easy to talk, very easy, isnt it? Here! would you like to know what my circumstances were?

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Yes: you had better tell me. Wont you sit down?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Oh, I'll sit down: dont you be afraid.
sp.stage: [She plants her chair farther forward with brazen energy, and sits down. Vivie is impressed in spite of herself].
sp.p: D'you know what your gran'mother was?

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: No, you dont. I do. She called herself a widow and had a fried-fish shop down by the Mint, and kept herself and four daughters out of it. Two of us were sisters: that was me and Liz; and we were both good-looking and well made. I suppose our father was a well-fed man: mother pretended he was a gentleman; but I dont know. The other two were only half sisters: undersized, ugly, starved looking, hard working, honest poor creatures: Liz and I would have half-murdered them if mother hadnt half-murdered u s to keep our hands off them. They were the respectable ones. Well, what did they get by their respectability? I'll tell you. One of them worked in a whitelead factory twelve hours a day for nine shillings a week until she died of lead poisoning. She only expected to get her hands a little paralyzed; but she died. The other was always held up to us as a model because she married a Government laborer in the Deptford victualling yard, and kept his room and the three children neat and tidy on eighteen shillings a week—until he took to drink. That was worth being respectable for, wasnt it?

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: Did you and your sister think so?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Liz didnt, I can tell you: she had more spirit. We both went to a church school—that was part of the ladylike airs we gave ourselves to be superior to the children that knew nothing and went nowhere—and we stayed there until Liz went out one night and never came back. I know the schoolmistress thought I'd soon follow her example; for the clergyman was always warning me that Lizzie'd end by jumping off Waterloo Bridge. Poor fool: that was all he knew about it! But I was more afraid of the whitelead factory than I was of the river; and so would you have been in my place. That clergyman got me a situation as scullery maid in a temperance restaurant where they sent out for anything you liked. Then I was waitress; and then I went to the bar at Waterloo station: fourteen hours a day serving drinks and washing glasses for four shillings a week and my board. That was considered a great promotion for me. Well, one cold, wretched night, when I was so tired I could hardly keep myself awake, who should come up for a half of Scotch but Lizzie, in a long fur cloak, elegant and comfortable, with a lot of sovereigns in her purse.

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: My aunt Lizzie!

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Yes; and a very good aunt to have, too. She's living down at Winchester now, close to the cathedral, one of the most respectable ladies there. Chaperones girls at the county ball, if you please. No river for Liz, thank you! You remind me of Liz a little: she was a first-rate business woman—saved money from the beginning—never let herself look too like what she was—never lost her head or threw away a chance. When she saw I'd grown up good-looking she said to me across the bar ‘What are you doing there, you little fool? wearing out your health and your appearance for other people's profit!’ Liz was saving money then to take a house for herself in Brussels; and she thought we two could save faster than one. So she lent me some money and gave me a start; and I saved steadily and first paid her back, and then went into business with her as her partner. Why shouldnt I have done it? The house in Brussels was real high class: a much better place for a woman to be in than the factory where Anne Jane got poisoned. None of our girls were ever treated as I was treated in the scullery of that temperance place, or at the Waterloo bar, or at home. Would you have had me stay in them and become a worn out old drudge before I was forty?

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: No; but why did you choose that business? Saving money and good management will succeed in any business.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Yes, saving money. But where can a woman get the money to save in any other business? Could you save out of four shillings a week and keep yourself dressed as well? Not you. Of course, if youre a plain woman and cant earn anything more; or if you have a turn for music, or the stage, or newspaper-writing: thats different. But neither Liz nor I had any turn for such things: all we had was our appearance and our turn for pleasing men. Do you think we were such fools as to let other people trade in our good looks by employing us as shopgirls, or barmaids, or waitresses, when we could trade in them ourselves and get all the profits instead of starvation wages? Not likely.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: You were certainly quite justified—from the business point of view.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Yes; or any other point of view. What is any respectable girl brought up to do but to catch some rich man's fancy and get the benefit of his money by marrying him?—as if a marriage ceremony could make any difference in the right or wrong of the thing! Oh, the hypocrisy of the world makes me sick! Liz and I had to work and save and calculate just like other people; elseways we should be as poor as any good-for-nothing drunken waster of a woman that thinks her luck will last for ever.
I despise such people: theyve no character; and if theres a thing I hate in a woman, its want of character.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Come now, mother: frankly! Isnt it part of what you call character in a woman that she should greatly dislike such a way of making money?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Why, of course. Everybody dislikes having to work and make money; but they have to do it all the same. I'm sure Ive often pitied a poor girl, tired out and in low spirits, having to try to please some man that she doesnt care two straws for—some half-drunken fool that thinks he's making himself agreeable when he's teasing and worrying and disgusting a woman so that hardly any money could pay her for putting up with it. But she has to bear with disagreeables and take the rough with the smooth, just like a nurse in a hospital or anyone else. It's not work that any woman would do for pleasure, goodness knows; though to hear the pious people talk you would suppose it was a bed of roses.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Still, you consider it worth while. It pays.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Of course it's worth while to a poor girl, if she can resist temptation and is good-looking and well conducted and sensible. It's far better than any other employment open to her. I always thought that oughtnt to be. It cant be right, Vivie, that there shouldnt be better opportunities for women. I stick to that: it's wrong. But it's so, right or wrong; and a girl must make the best of it. But of course it's not worth while for a lady. If you took to it youd be a fool; but I should have been a fool if I'd taken to anything else.

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: Mother: suppose we were both as poor as you were in those wretched old days, are you quite sure that you wouldnt advise me to try the Waterloo bar, or marry a laborer, or even go into the factory?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Of course not. What sort of mother do you take me for! How could you keep your self-respect in such starvation and slavery? And whats a woman worth? whats life worth? without self-respect! Why am I independent and able to give my daughter a first-rate education, when other women that had just as good opportunities are in the gutter? Because I always knew how to respect myself and control myself. Why is Liz looked up to in a cathedral town? The same reason. Where would we be now if we'd minded the clergyman's foolishness? Scrubbing floors for one and sixpence a day and nothing to look forward to but the workhouse infirmary. Dont you be led astray by people who dont know the world, my girl. The only way for a woman to provide for herself decently is for her to be good to some man that can afford to be good to her. If she's in his own station of life, let her make him marry her; but if she's far beneath him she cant expect it: why should she? it wouldnt be for her own happiness. Ask any lady in London society that has daughters; and she'll tell you the same, except that I tell you straight and she'll tell you crooked. Thats all the difference.

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: My dear mother: you are a wonderful woman: you are stronger than all England. And are you really and truly not one wee bit doubtful—or—or—ashamed?

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: Well, of course, dearie, it's only good manners to be ashamed of it: it's expected from a woman. Women have to pretend to feel a great deal that they dont feel. Liz used to be angry with me for plumping out the truth about it. She used to say that when every woman could learn enough from what was going on in the world before her eyes, there was no need to talk about it to her. But then Liz was such a perfect lady! She had the true instinct of it; while I was always a bit of a vulgarian. I used to be so pleased when you sent me your photos to see that you were growing up like Liz: youve just her ladylike, determined way. But I cant stand saying one thing when everyone knows I mean another. Whats the use in such hypocrisy? If people arrange the world that way for women, theres no good pretending it's arranged the other way. No: I never was a bit ashamed really. I consider I had a right to be proud of how we managed everything so respectably, and never had a word against us, and how the girls were so well taken care of. Some of them did very well: one of them married an ambassador. But of course now I darent talk about such things: whatever would they think of us!
Oh dear! I do believe I'm getting sleepy after all.
sp.stage: [She stretches herself lazily, thoroughly relieved by her explosion, and placidly ready for her night's rest].

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: I believe it is I who will not be able to sleep now.
sp.stage: [She goes to the dresser and lights the candle. Then she extinguishes the lamp, darkening the room a good deal].
sp.p: Better let in some fresh air before locking up.
sp.stage: [She opens the cottage door, and finds that it is broad moonlight].
sp.p: What a beautiful night! Look!
sp.stage: [She draws aside the curtains of the window. The landscape is seen bathed in the radiance of the harvest moon rising over Blackdown].

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.stage: [with a perfunctory glance at the scene]
sp.p: Yes, dear; but take care you dont catch your death of cold from the night air.

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: Nonsense.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Oh yes: everything I say is nonsense, according to you.

sp.speaker: VIVIE
sp.p: No: really that is not so, mother. You have got completely the better of me tonight, though I intended it to be the other way. Let us be good friends now.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: So it has been the other way. But I suppose I must give in to it. I always got the worst of it from Liz; and now I suppose it'll be the same with you.

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: Well, never mind. Come: goodnight, dear old mother.
sp.stage: [She takes her mother in her arms].

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: I brought you up well, didnt I, dearie?

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: You did.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN.
sp.p: And youll be good to your poor old mother for it, wont you?

sp.speaker: VIVIE.
sp.p: I will, dear.
Goodnight.

sp.speaker: MRS WARREN
sp.p: Blessings on my own dearie darling! a mother's blessing!

div.stage: She embraces her daughter protectingly, instinctively looking upward for divine sanction.

div.head: ACT III
div.stage: In the Rectory garden next morning, with the sun shining from a cloudless sky. The garden wall has a five-barred wooden gate, wide enough to admit a carriage, in the middle. Beside the gate hangs a bell on a coiled spring, communicating with a pull outside. The carriage drive comes down the middle of the garden and then swerves to its left, where it ends in a little gravelled circus opposite the Rectory porch. Beyond the gate is seen the dusty high road, parallel with the wall, bounded on the farther side by a strip of turf and an unfenced pine wood. On the lawn, between the house and the drive, is a clipped yew tree, with a garden bench in its shade. On the opposite side the garden is shut in by a box hedge; and there is a sundial on the turf, with an iron chair near it. A little path leads off through the box hedge, behind the sundial. Frank, seated on the chair near the sundial, on which he has placed the morning papers, is reading The Standard. His father comes from the house, red-eyed and shivery, and meets Frank's eye with misgiving.

sp.speaker: FRANK
sp.p: Half-past eleven. Nice hour for a rector to come down to breakfast!

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Dont mock, Frank: dont mock. I am a little—er—

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Off color?

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: No, sir: unwell this morning. Wheres your mother?

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Dont be alarmed: she's not here. Gone to town by the 11.13 with Bessie. She left several messages for you. Do you feel equal to receiving them now, or shall I wait til youve breakfasted?

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: I have breakfasted, sir. I am surprised at your mother going to town when we have people staying with us. Theyll think it very strange.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Possibly she has considered that. At all events, if Crofts is going to stay here, and you are going to sit up every night with him until four, recalling the incidents of your fiery youth, it is clearly my mother's duty, as a prudent housekeeper, to go up to the stores and order a barrel of whisky and a few hundred siphons.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: I did not observe that Sir George drank excessively.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: You were not in a condition to, gov'nor.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Do you mean to say that I—?

sp.speaker: FRANK
sp.p: I never saw a beneficed clergyman less sober. The anecdotes you told about your past career were so awful that I really dont think Praed would have passed the night under your roof if it hadnt been for the way my mother and he took to one another.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Nonsense, sir. I am Sir George Crofts' host. I must talk to him about something; and he has only one subject. Where is Mr Praed now?

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: He is driving my mother and Bessie to the station.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Is Crofts up yet?

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Oh, long ago. He hasnt turned a hair: he's in much better practice than you. He has kept it up ever since, probably. He's taken himself off somewhere to smoke.

div.stage: Frank resumes his paper. The parson turns disconsolately towards the gate; then comes back irresolutely.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Er—Frank.

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Do you think the Warrens will expect to be asked here after yesterday afternoon?

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Theyve been asked already.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: What!!!

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Crofts informed us at breakfast that you told him to bring Mrs Warren and Vivie over here today, and to invite them to make this house their home. My mother then found she must go to town by the 11.13 train.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: I never gave any such invitation. I never thought of such a thing.

sp.speaker: FRANK
sp.p: How do you know, gov'nor, what you said and thought last night?

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: Good morning.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
sp.p: Good morning. I must apologise for not having met you at breakfast. I have a touch of—of—

sp.speaker: FRANK.
sp.p: Clergyman's sore throat, Praed. Fortunately not chronic.

sp.speaker: PRAED
sp.p: Well, I must say your house is in a charming spot here. Really most charming.

sp.speaker: REV. S.
